question: What did Jesus teach about the Law?
aliases: do Christians have to keep the law
finding: Jesus was a Torah-observant Jewish teacher who intensified the Law's ethical core and subordinated its cultic and purity apparatus to that core. He never abolished it and never declared it void; he ranked it. Where ritual and mercy collide, mercy is what the ritual was for. That is not antinomianism and not abolition; it is a recognizably Jewish prophetic argument conducted inside the covenant. It matters for everything else on these cards, because it means the "faith versus works" frame was never Jesus's question. His question was never whether to keep Torah. It was which part of it is load-bearing, and he answered out loud, more than once, with justice, mercy and faithfulness.
oneLiners: He didn't lower the bar. Read Matthew 5:20: the Pharisees weren't righteous enough.
"Weightier matters of the law." That's a comparative, inside the law, in his own mouth.
Finish the verse: "and not to leave the other undone." He never said stop tithing.
He sends the leper to the priest and never sends anyone to the altar for forgiveness. Both of those are true, and together they're the whole argument.
Marcion abolished the Law. Paul relativized it. Jesus intensified it. Three different positions, and we're on the third.
doNotSay: Never cite Matthew 23:23 without its last clause. Someone who knows the text will finish the verse for you.
Don't rest Mark 7 on "it's Mark's aside." The underlying saying is early (Thomas 14, Q/Luke 10:8) and we accept it. The principle is about ritual defilement, not ethics.
Don't say Jesus addressed Gentiles on Sabbath and food laws. He didn't. James did (Acts 15), and the Didache gives a graduated answer.
Don't pretend Jesus voided Torah. The leper verse wrecks that reading, which is our reading's opponent, not ours.

boardLabels.other: THE OTHER STACK · the earliest Jewish-Christian reading

sources.note: Not to abolish but to fulfil; not one jot or tittle passes; and "except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees." The problem with the Pharisees is not enough righteousness. Then the Sermon makes every commandment harder: murder → anger, adultery → the look, eye for eye → no retaliation.

sources.phrase: one tittle of the law to fail
sources.note: The jot-and-tittle saying is in Luke independently, which puts it in Q, upstream of both evangelists. Our method keeps it against our interest.

sources.tier: red text · the thesis in one verse
sources.phrase: and not to leave the other undone
sources.note: Weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, faith. A comparative, inside the law. And the final clause forecloses the antinomian reading: he does not tell them to stop tithing herbs. Quote the last clause every time.

sources.phrase: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice
sources.note: A Sabbath halakhic dispute settled by a prophet's ranking principle. He is not waving the Law off; he is arguing a case within it, from scripture, the way a Jewish teacher argues.

sources.phrase: The sabbath was made for man
sources.note: He defends the grain-plucking from David and the shewbread (1 Samuel 21): a Torah precedent. Legal reasoning, not dismissal. He states the day's purpose; he does not abolish it.

sources.phrase: to do good on the sabbath days
sources.note: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?" The position that human need overrides ritual obligation is a position in Jewish law, with rabbinic parallels.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 27
sources.phrase: observe the Sabbath as a Sabbath
sources.note: Thomas keeps the Sabbath as a live category, independently.

sources.phrase: Thou art not far from the kingdom of God
sources.note: Both halves of the greatest commandment are quotations from Torah (Deuteronomy 6:4-5; Leviticus 19:18). The scribe adds that this is "more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices," and Jesus commends him. An argument among Jews about Torah, not a repudiation of it.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 6, 53, 89
sources.note: Asked about fasting, prayer, alms, diet (6), circumcision (53), washing the cup (89), he redirects to the interior every time. Thomas 53 does not say circumcision is sin; it relocates it. Relocation, not abolition. That is the pattern everywhere.

sources.tier: red text · triple-attested · the hardest text on the card
sources.phrase: offer the gift that Moses commanded
sources.note: He puts a healed man into the sacrificial system. Concede it completely. It is a civil-status statute (Leviticus 13-14: the priest certifies reentry), "for a testimony unto them," and it wrecks the "Jesus abolished the Law" reading. Then the line that matters: he never once sends anyone to the Temple to purchase forgiveness. Civil statute obeyed; sin-atonement machinery bypassed (Mark 2:5; Luke 7:48).

sources.tier: red text · earliest gospel · Mark's aside
sources.note: "Thus he declared all foods clean." The clause is Mark's aside; Matthew copies the pericope (15:1-20) and the comment isn't there. But don't rest on that: the underlying saying is early and we accept it (Thomas 14; Q/Luke 10:8). It is about ritual defilement, not ethics: the question was handwashing. A thing can be ritually clean and still be wrong to do.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 14
sources.phrase: what goes into your mouth will not defile you
sources.note: The purity principle, independently attested. Our case about killing animals was never a kosher case; it is a non-harm case built on Isaiah 66:3, Hosea 6:6 and the Temple action. Acts 15's four decrees are a restriction on killing and blood, not a kosher code either.

sources.tier: red text · the tension inside one gospel
sources.note: "Do whatever they teach you" vs. Matthew 15's attack on their tradition. The tension resolves on a distinction Jesus draws: 23:2-3 affirms the seat and the next thirty verses attack the occupants; 15:1-20 contests the paradosis, the handed-down tradition, and defends written Torah against it (15:6). Written Torah affirmed; scribal accretion contested; hypocrisy flayed.

sources.phrase: of none effect by your tradition
sources.note: "Ye have made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition." Korban vows and handwashing. He defends the written law against the superstructure.

sources.title: Didache 6:2-3
sources.note: "So are Christians obligated to keep the Sabbath and the food laws?" Jesus never addressed Gentiles on this; James did (Acts 15), and the oldest church manual gives a graduated answer: bear what you can of the yoke; about food, undertake what you can; keep strictly from idol-meat. A floor and a direction of travel.

sources.title: Recognitions 1.36, sacrifice as a concession
sources.note: Moses "allowed them indeed to sacrifice, but permitted it to be done only to God, that by any means he might cut off one half of the deeply ingrained evil." Second-century Jewish Christianity read Jesus as a Torah-ranker: the ethical core is the law, the cult a concession.

sources.title: Homilies 3.51 on Matthew 5:17
sources.phrase: did not belong to the law
sources.note: "The things which He destroyed did not belong to the law." This reading is not a 21st-century invention.
